vignette:
Arjun sits in the armchair across from me, his posture precise—shoulders squared, hands resting on his knees. He is a junior diplomat, recently reassigned to a desk job at the ministry’s headquarters after two years in a conflict zone. He speaks in measured sentences, his accent smooth, but his eyes move constantly: to the window, to the door, to the corner of the room. He apologizes for this, says it’s a habit he can’t shake. When I ask how long it has been happening, he pauses. “Since the siege,” he says.

He was posted to a small embassy in a city that became a war zone. For the first six months, his work involved cultural liaison—arranging meetings, writing reports, attending receptions. Then the insurgents took the airport. Mortar fire became a nightly rhythm. He describes the sound as something that lived in his chest, a pressure before the explosion. He learned to sleep in the embassy basement with the other staff, pressed against concrete walls, a single bottle of water between them. He remembers the fear less as a feeling and more as a constant hum, like a generator running under his skin.

The event that broke him happened in the embassy’s courtyard. A car bomb detonated outside the perimeter wall. He was standing near the gate, waiting for a courier. The blast threw him sideways, and when he opened his eyes, the guard who had been standing next to him was gone. Not dead—just gone. He learned later that the man had been blown across the street. Arjun helped carry the wounded into the building, his hands shaking, his ears ringing. That night, he could not stop seeing the empty space where the guard had been. He thought: *That could have been me.* He thought: *It should have been me.*

Now he works in a high-rise office building with tinted windows and silent elevators. He tells me he cannot sit with his back to the door. He checks the parking garage every morning for unattended vehicles. He replays the blast in his head during meetings, the sound of glass raining down, the smell of diesel and blood. He has become irritable with his girlfriend, a lawyer who tries to comfort him. He knows he is snapping at her, but he cannot stop. When she touches him unexpectedly, he flinches. Sometimes he wakes up in the dark, his heart hammering, convinced he hears the whistle of an incoming shell. The bedroom ceiling looks exactly like the basement ceiling in the embassy—same cracks, same shadows. He avoids crowds, but as a diplomat, he cannot skip receptions. So he goes, stands near the exit, and counts the seconds until he can leave.

He says he feels hollow, like the bomb took something out of him that won’t grow back. He stopped reading the news. He stopped calling his mother in Delhi because he doesn’t want her to worry. He has nightmares three or four times a week—always the same: he is back in the courtyard, the guard is there, then he isn’t, and Arjun is standing alone, waiting for the next blast. He has started drinking before bed, just enough to numb the edges. He knows this is not sustainable. He knows he needs help. That is why he came. But sitting here, in this quiet room, he tells me he does not know if talking will change anything. The war is over for the city, he says. But for him, it is still happening. Every day. Every night. Right now.
